newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl under fire from unions for pay proposal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl under fire from unions for pay proposal.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, touching a raw nerve with unions angry at record unemployment, said on Wednesday that Germans should accept little or no real wage increases over the next few years in a bid to create jobs.

Kohl told Germany's Bild newspaper his proposal did not mean real cuts "but merely doing without growth in prosperity" and that Bonn's bid to get Germany into Europe's currency union did not conflict with his aim of boosting employment.

"I find it absolutely reasonable that everyone who has a job should for a few years curb their demands or even completely do without a real increase in wages so that the employment chances for those who are unemployed will improve," Kohl told the mass-circulation newspaper.

Several German union leaders quickly condemned Kohl's proposal, saying workers over the past few years had seen virtually no real wage increases because of rising tax rates and mounting social-security contributions implemented by Bonn.

Economists said Kohl's proposal reflected increasing frustration over Germany's failure to cap joblessness, particularly after last week's news that unemployment surged to a new post-war record of 4.66 million in January.
"I think this proposal shows the Kohl government is pretty desperate for solutions," said Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt.
"Many people still remember his pledge that we would see blossoming landscapes in eastern Germany a few years after unification," he said.

Unions stepped up demands that Kohl's ruling Christian Democratic Union coalition stop protecting employers -- who they claim have failed to fulfil long-standing promises to add workers -- and boost public spending that has been slashed to reduce the federal budget deficit.

"Profits and share prices keep rising, exports hum along and unemployment also just keeps on rising," said IG Metall leader Klaus Zwickel said, noting German unemployment has doubled since Kohl took office in 1982.
Union leaders also decried that regular workers were being forced to bear the brunt of Bonn's efforts to whip Germany's finances into shape to join currency union in January 1999.
"The unions have done enough. It is time for employers and the government to act," said Herbert Mai, president of the OeTV public-sector workers' union.
